title: The Well of the Undercroft
premise: Sable Thornbury returns to Hollowmere House to appraise it for a bank, only to find her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, waiting on the porch — real, unchanged, and terrified. The house is a well that feeds on sung devotion: generations of families have vanished into its undercroft, lured by a lullaby whose final verse was never written down. Sable must recover the last verse from the memories of the house's previous victims without ever singing along, while the found family of survivors hiding in its walls teaches her that love can be a weapon against duty. In the end she refuses to complete the song, sings a verse of her own making instead, and collapses the well — saving Wren and the others at the cost of the house, her inheritance, and the version of herself who never believed.
about_author: Mara Oyelaran is a former building inspector turned horror writer who spent a decade cataloguing condemned properties across the American Midwest. She writes about houses the way other people write about exes: with dread, tenderness, and an unshakeable conviction that they remember everything.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. She arrives at Hollowmere House with a clipboard and a firm disbelief in anything uncanny, tasked with valuing a property no bank wants to touch. The measurements refuse to add up; rooms are larger inside than out. The emotional beat is professional detachment beginning to crack as the house seems to take note of her arrival.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. On the porch sits Wren, the imaginary friend she invented at age six — aged not a day, humming a tune Sable hasn't heard in thirty years. Wren warns her not to go past the cellar door. The beat is vertigo: the collapse of Sable's rational worldview, and the first stirrings of an old, fierce protectiveness.

chapters.title: The People in the Walls
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, shifting to ensemble. She discovers survivors living in the house's sealed servant corridors: Odile, a former owner's daughter; Tam and Ruthie, siblings born inside. They explain the well beneath the undercroft and the lullaby that feeds it. The beat is wary found-family formation — suspicion giving way to shared bread and shared fear.

chapters.title: What the Well Wants
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A history of the house: every generation, one member hears the full song and walks down willingly, loved ones following. The last verse has always been lost because no singer survives to teach it. The beat is grief and duty — Odile believes someone must finally finish the song to free them all, and she's chosen Sable.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Training montage with teeth: Ruthie teaches Sable the known verses so she'll recognize the trap, while Wren grows weaker each time the house hums through the walls. Sable realizes the song works through love — it needs you to want to sing along. The beat is mounting dread entwined with deepening bonds.

chapters.title: Tam Goes Down
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Tam, exhausted and homesick for a world he's never seen, begins humming the melody in his sleep. One night he's simply gone, the cellar door standing open. The beat is devastating loss and guilt — proof the house doesn't wait for volunteers forever, and that time has run out.

chapters.title: The Undercroft
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Against everyone's advice, Sable descends to find Tam, navigating a stairwell that lengthens when unloved and shortens when accompanied. She finds the well itself: a throat of dark water that echoes back your own voice, slightly ahead of you. The beat is terror sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, intercut with Wren's. At the well's edge, the house offers Sable the final verse through Tam's voice and then her mother's. She nearly sings along — until Wren arrives and sings the wrong words, loudly, lovingly, breaking the spell. The beat is the climax: love against duty, refusal as salvation.

chapters.title: A Song of Her Own
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Sable improvises a new ending — a graceless, human verse about mortgages and burnt toast and staying — and the well, built to receive completion, cannot digest it. The house groans, floods upward, and begins to come down around them. The beat is chaotic, triumphant escape as the found family runs together.

chapters.title: Market Value
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Weeks later, Sable files her appraisal: the property is condemned, worthless, perfect. Wren, freed with the house's fall, is fading gently but chooses to stay near Sable a little longer. The survivors keep in touch over Sunday dinners. The beat is bittersweet resolution — survival cost everything except what mattered.
